title: App requests and toolkit types
text: App Requests and Toolkits are two separate controls over what members can reach: which catalog applications a project is allowed to use, and which toolkit types exist on the deployment at all. Decide an app request A member who opens the application catalog and requests access to something their project is not configured for creates a row here — separate from the agent/skill publishing review, which is a different mechanism entirely. The queue lists pending requests with who asked and for what. Both record your decision and notify the requester in the same transaction. Approving a request records the decision and tells the requester — it does not itself grant anything. Nothing in the platform reads an approved row and automatically unlocks a capability; whether the requested application actually becomes usable depends on whether its toolkit type is enabled for that project, below. Control which toolkit types are offered Open Toolkits . This decides, per toolkit type, whether it is enabled, disabled, or restricted to named projects — always with a reason and a recorded decider. The table lists every catalogue type with its current availability and a worker support indicator. Choose enabled, disabled, or restricted; a restricted type also lists which projects can use it. A reason is required for every choice except reverting to the default. This page does not add a new toolkit type. A pre built MCP server becomes a type through Configuration's MCP Servers section, and an external provider's toolkits would arrive through Service Descriptors — a third registration path here would be a third thing to keep synchronized. The worker column is advisory: it reports whether the toolkit type is known to run on the deployment's configured worker, not whether the type is disallowed. Elitea can run its agent runtime on either a Python worker (the default for both Helm and compose, 865/ 866) or a Rust worker (opt in), and their toolkit coverage differs: Choosing the Rust worker hides 18 toolkit types that only run on the Python worker (for example Jira, Confluence, TestRail, Bitbucket, and several others — GitHub itself is one of the Rust worker's 22 supported families, not one of the hidden ones) — tracked in 865. Python worker default fails to import 9 toolkit types with no supported substitute on this worker ( aws , azure , azure search , bigquery , delta lake , gcp , k8s , localgit , yagmail ). Google Places, Rally, ServiceNow and Slack used to be on this list too; they import cleanly as of 869. Check which worker your deployment runs before assuming a type's tile will actually work.

title: Audit trail
text: Audit Trail is a read only view over what happened on the deployment — there is nothing to edit or configure here. Use it to answer "who did this, and when," whether you are investigating an incident, confirming a change actually landed, or checking whether a scheduled job ran. Review activity User events are actions a person took; System events are platform generated (for example a scheduled job firing). Each has its own tab. Narrow by date range (with quick presets like 30 minutes, today, yesterday, 7 days, or 30 days, plus an explicit From/To), event type, project, user, or errors only. A calendar style heatmap shows activity density over time, so a spike is visible before you drill into individual events. Traces and spans A second view mode, alongside events, shows execution traces and their individual spans — each row names the action and, when there is one, the tool or model that ran it. Spans can be filtered by duration band (under 10 ms, up to over 10 seconds), which is the fastest way to find what is running slowly across the deployment rather than one conversation at a time. Investigate one person From the Users page's row menu, the activity drawer filters this same audit data to one account — useful when investigating a specific person's actions rather than browsing the whole trail. See Users and roles. This page has no write path of any kind. An audit trail the product could edit would not be one. Audit Trail records what happened; it does not enforce anything. If you are looking for the controls that decide who can do what in the first place, see Users and roles.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication lives under Configuration › Authentication in the admin console. It covers how people sign in (OIDC or SAML) and how an identity provider's groups map onto project membership (SCIM). Configure an identity provider The list shows any providers already configured, one live per protocol. Choose OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0 . Issuer URL (a .well known/openid configuration URL is accepted and reduced to its issuer), Client ID, client secret, redirect URI, scopes, and whether e mail verification is required. Identity provider entity ID, SSO URL, single logout URL, and certificate(s); this service's own entity ID and ACS URL; name ID format; the e mail and name attribute mappings; whether to sign AuthnRequests; the service provider certificate; and clock skew tolerance. Turning a provider on retires any other provider of the same protocol — only one live OIDC and one live SAML definition can exist at a time, because each protocol is served on one route. A stored secret is never shown in the clear — the field renders a mask, and there is no "reveal" control. To change it, enter a new value; leaving it blank keeps the existing one. Deleting a provider also deletes its stored secret, which cannot be recovered. To stop using a provider for new logins without losing its configuration, turn off "use this provider for logins" instead of deleting it. Bind SCIM groups to a project role SCIM lets an identity provider push its directory — creating and deactivating accounts as people join and leave — rather than only federating logins. The SCIM endpoint is /api/v2/scim/v2 , authenticated with a personal access token; configuring it in your identity provider is outside Elitea's UI. What the admin console does provide is the group to role mapping, beneath the identity provider list: Name the SCIM group exactly as your identity provider sends it, and choose the project and role it grants. A member the group granted the role to loses it when they leave the group. A member who already held that role independently keeps it — the identity provider is authoritative only over what it granted, not over everything it happens to find. A SCIM group with no binding is refused by name; it never creates a project on its own, and it never guesses a role.

title: Branding
text: Branding is a runtime setting, not a build step: changes reach every user on their next page load, with no rebuild or restart required. The brand pack you edit here is what the platform serves to every client on the deployment — there is no per project or per user brand. Edit the brand pack The form is grouped into identity, color/type/shape, assets, and font faces. Every field can inherit from the platform default instead of being set explicitly, and the form says what it would inherit and from where. Logos and other assets are uploaded directly; self hosted font faces are declared here rather than linked externally. A sample surface renders in both light and dark under a theme built from your current draft, including the derived color swatches and a text on primary contrast check. The check is a warning only — it does not block saving. The merged pack becomes what every user's next page load receives. Import, export, and restore a package Download the current brand as a package. Uploading a package runs a dry run first, so you see what would change before committing it. Kept versions can be restored from the package panel. An unsaved draft is respected by the import and restore controls — neither silently discards edits you have not saved yet. What is inherited by default Every branding field defaults to the platform's own look unless you override it. This means a fresh deployment already looks complete without any editing here — Branding is where you replace that default with your organization's identity, one field at a time, not something you must fully populate before it is usable.

title: Budgets and LLM governance
text: Budgets and LLM Governance are two separate admin pages that both shape how the LLM gateway treats a request. Set spend limits Open Budgets . Each row is a project or a project member with a spend ceiling. Search, then open its budget dialog. Choose a monthly limit, or mark it unlimited. The gateway bills on the calendar month; no other period is enforced. Choose whether the gateway fails open (allows calls through) or fails closed (refuses calls) if it cannot reach its budget counter, or inherit the platform default. Open the members drawer to set a spend ceiling for an individual project member, on top of the project ceiling. A budget stored here is only enforced if the LLM gateway is configured with GATEWAY NATS URL . Without it, every number on this page round trips and saves, but no call is ever refused for exceeding it. The page shows a warning only when the gateway itself reports enforcement is off — never from silence. The spend ceiling on this page is set per project and per member only — there is no per agent or per tool spend cap, and setting one is not planned. To see WHICH agent or tool a project's cost came from, open Settings › Analytics on the project and use the Costs tab's Cost by Agent and Cost by Tool tables ( 875). Author LLM governance rules Open LLM Governance . Each row is a scoped rule the gateway reads and enforces on the /llm path: budgets, rate limits, model and MCP server allowlists, credential rate policy, and CEL based routing rules. Choose the scope it applies to (provider, model, or project) and the rule fields for that scope. A saved definition does not take effect immediately — the gateway polls this table on a refresh interval (30 seconds by default) rather than reloading on every write, so a replica that missed an event still converges. A saved rule can still be unenforceable: it may fail to load, or load and match nothing it could ever apply to. The gateway's own status report (surfaced on the LLM proxy Status tab) names any rule it rejected — a save here is not proof the rule is in force.

title: Features and configuration
text: Features and Configuration are two admin pages that share one mechanism: a list of sections, each either editable here or pointing you to where it actually lives. A section that this deployment cannot serve says so, with a reason, instead of rendering a form that saves into nothing. Features Whether Elitea exposes an MCP server at all, and whether MCP servers show in the main navigation. Block agent publishing platform wide, restrict it to named projects, and set the categories offered. The same three controls, for skills. Turn on the project Analytics tab (Settings › Analytics). The links shown on the in app Help Center page. Enable the assistant, and set which project and agent answer it. Turn voice input and text to speech on, or keep the controls visible but disabled. From the list on the left. Only changed fields are sent; Discard reverts unsaved edits. Configuration Configuration holds the sections Features does not: some editable directly here, some pointing to a dedicated page. Blocked toolkit types (a blocked type cannot be listed or created, and is stripped from every agent before it runs — existing toolkits of that type stay visible so an administrator can review and delete them, but stop working); blocked individual tools within an otherwise allowed toolkit; tools that require the user to authorize each call ("sensitive action" tools, matched per toolkit or with for every toolkit); the company name and message template shown in that authorization dialog. A dismissible banner shown across the app, with its own icon, style, and message. Turns on maintenance mode: every caller without administration access gets a 503 and the splash screen, with its own title, message, and optional HTML. The admin console and authentication routes stay reachable so the window is reversible from inside itself. The outbound mail relay: SMTP host, port, TLS mode, credentials, from/reply to addresses, and the public base URL used in links the platform sends. Environment variables ( SMTP HOST and its siblings) provide a second layer underneath these rows; a row set here wins over the environment field by field. These sections carry credentials or need a row editor shape a flat form cannot express, so each is a page of its own: see Authentication, LLM proxy, and Branding. MCP Servers configures the pre built MCP server catalogue; see the MCP integration guides for what that catalogue offers. Stays unavailable on this page specifically, because a governance corpus is a list of scoped rules rather than one value document. See Budgets and LLM governance. A registry for external provider integrations. This deployment publishes none, so the page reports that rather than showing an empty grid. Configuration's "Advanced", "Observability", "Runtime", and "Admin Panel" sections from the legacy admin UI have no counterpart here — their fields addressed process environment variables and mounted files that no form could ever write, so they were removed rather than kept as permanently unavailable placeholders.

title: LLM proxy
text: The LLM Proxy screen lives under Configuration › LLM Proxy in the admin console. It is the platform wide control over the LLM gateway that sits in front of every model call, organized into six tabs. Whether the gateway is reachable, and whether rate limits and budgets are actually enforceable right now. The platform model catalogue and its per project grants. Deployment wide spend by provider and model. A per request log of every call the gateway served. Publish a provider credential once for the whole platform. The default soft alert threshold for budget warnings. Publish a provider platform wide Normally an AI provider credential belongs to one project. Providers & models lets you publish one from the public project instead, so every project can use it without configuring its own copy. Existing platform providers are listed with a status ok indicator — the gateway only ever dispatches to a provider whose endpoint and key resolve, so a row reporting status ok = false is stored and listed but silently never used. Same provider types as a project credential (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, EPAM DIAL, Anthropic, Ollama, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, vLLM). A row imported from an older deployment can still hold its key as plain text rather than sealed in the vault. The panel flags this as sealed: false without ever displaying the value; re saving the credential through this screen seals it. Grant a platform model to specific projects Under Models , each platform model carries a share scope: All projects — every project on the deployment can use it (the default for any model saved before this control existed). No project — stored and listed, but offered nowhere. Selected projects — offered only to the team projects you pick. Personal projects are not offered here individually — granting to one would be a grant to a single person, which this screen does not do. Choose the share scope, and for Selected projects , search and pick which team projects. The model becomes available (or unavailable) to the chosen projects' model pickers. credential resolves = false on a model means it names a provider this platform does not currently publish (or none). That, like status ok = false , means the model is stored and listed but never actually served — this screen is where you see why. Read status, usage, logs, and alerts Reports what the gateway currently holds, not what was last saved — a governance rule can be rejected at load, or load but match nothing, and neither looks different from the authoring side. If the gateway is unreachable, the panel says so rather than showing stale numbers as if they were live. Reads the per request billing ledger, deployment wide, broken down by provider and model. This is a report, not a control — nothing here enforces a budget; that happens on Budgets and governance. Reads every request the gateway served, including ones a billing based Usage report would miss entirely — refused by a budget, rejected by policy, sent to an unresolvable model, or failed upstream. The log has no column for a prompt, completion, or upstream error text; the panel states that rather than showing an expandable row with nothing in it. One deployment wide default soft alert percentage for budget warnings. A project with its own alert threshold keeps using that value — changing the default here does not override it. Turning alerting off stops the warning only; the gateway still bills and still refuses a call that exceeds a budget. Retries, timeouts, fallback chains, key weighting, and semantic caching are not configurable from here or anywhere else in the product — the gateway runs its defaults for all of them.

title: Admin console overview
text: The admin console is a separate application at /admin/app , distinct from the main Elitea app. It is where an administrator manages the deployment as a whole: users, projects, authentication, the LLM proxy, budgets, branding, and platform wide configuration. Open the admin console Sign in to Elitea normally, then navigate to /admin/app . The console renders only if your account holds at least one administration mode permission — otherwise you see an access denied screen instead of an empty shell. Every individual page still enforces its own permission on the server on every request; the console's own check only decides whether it is worth rendering the navigation at all. Navigation groups The sidebar has two groups. Delete, promote, suspend, and review activity for any account. The permission matrix, across the central, public, and support scopes. Suspend, create, delete, and manage membership for every project. The global secret vault, merged into every project. Application access requests waiting on a decision. Authentication, LLM Proxy, MCP servers, banner, maintenance, e mail, and more, as a set of schema driven sections. The white label pack — colors, assets, and fonts. The outbound mail relay. Feature toggles: MCP exposure, publishing, analytics, Help Center, Support Assistant, Voice. A read only provider registry; most of it reports "not available" rather than data. Which toolkit types this deployment offers, and to which projects. Budgets, rate limits, allowlists, credential policy, and routing rules the LLM gateway enforces. Per project and per member spend limits. The deployment wide record of what happened. Cron schedules and background job status. There is no LiteLLM section. LiteLLM has been replaced by a standalone gateway service; its former admin screen is gone rather than kept as a dead link. A "Service Descriptors" entry is present even though the legacy admin UI never linked to it — it now answers honestly that this platform has no external provider hub, which is more useful than a page nothing could reach. What each page can and cannot decide window injected permission flags in the console are presentation only: they decide what the sidebar shows, never what a request is allowed to do. Every read and write is re authorized on the server against the actual permission that route requires. A typed URL to a page your account cannot use still reaches it — and still gets refused there.

title: Projects
text: The admin Projects page is the deployment wide project list. Every project — team or personal — appears here, regardless of who owns it. This is the one place an administrator sees and acts on every project at once, rather than one project's own Settings page at a time. Manage an existing project Search the table by name. A suspended project's members lose access until it is unsuspended. Both are available from the project's row menu. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Create or delete a project Both actions run a multi step process rather than a single database write: creating a project provisions its record, quota, dedicated schema, permission set, a system user and token, vault secrets, storage buckets, and vector store together; deleting one reverses the same steps, ending in dropping the project's schema. Each step's status is tracked individually, and a failed attempt is compensated rather than left half applied. Deleting a project destroys its data irreversibly. There is no undo. Approving a member's project request A member does not have to ask you directly. From the project switcher, + Request a project opens a small form — a name and a justification — that files a request the same way the App Requests moderation pattern already handles application access (see App requests and toolkit types). It lands on this same App Requests page , under the "Project Request" issue type. On App Requests, set the Issue Type filter to Project Request . Approve runs the same multi step creation process described above — schema, permissions, vault, the lot — with the requester made the new project's admin. Reject requires a reason, exactly like any other app request, and creates nothing. Approving names the new project's id in the queue and in the requester's notification; rejecting delivers your reason. Unlike every other request this queue handles, approving a "Project Request" is not clerical: it is the one decision on this page that creates something rather than only recording an answer.

title: Schedules and tasks
text: Two admin pages cover recurring and running work: Schedules & Tasks for cron schedules, and Tasks for a live view of background jobs. Manage schedules Open Schedules & Tasks . Its Schedules tab lists cron bound platform jobs (for example, indexing schedules) with a live read and write — the scheduler service polls this table every minute and dispatches whatever is due. Each row pairs a cron expression with the platform operation it runs. Disabling a row stops it from being dispatched without deleting it. Open a schedule's history drawer for its past occurrences. The page's own "Tasks" tab is a permanent notice, not a table: it describes maintenance operations from the legacy plugin runtime, which this platform does not have and has no plan to add. It answers as unavailable rather than as an empty list, so "nothing is running" and "this deployment cannot see what is running" are never shown identically. See what is running Open the separate Tasks page for a live view of background work this platform actually tracks: index runs, agent turns, toolkit tool calls, scheduled occurrences, and evaluation runs. Narrow the list to one kind of task. The cancel control only appears on rows the server reports as cancellable — a task past that point does not offer it, rather than offering a control that would mostly answer with a conflict. There is no start control and no log tail here. Starting a task and reading its output are not modeled by this page — a task's output is its own artifact rather than a live log stream.

title: Secrets
text: Admin Secrets is a different store from a project's own Settings › Secrets page. A project's vault serves only that project; the global vault edited here is merged into {{secret.…}} resolution for every project on the deployment. Use the global vault for a value every project should be able to reference — a shared API key for an internal tool, a company wide webhook target — instead of copying the same secret into each project's own vault, where it would need to be kept in sync by hand. Manage a global secret The table lists every global secret by key; values are masked. Give it a key and a value. Reference it from any project as {{secret. }} , the same placeholder syntax used for a project scoped secret. A write here is platform wide — it changes what every project resolves for that key. There is no "hide" control for a global secret. A masked value already hides the secret; a separate hide action exists on neither this page nor its server route. The Internal tab is read only for every administrator, including super admins. It groups entries the platform wrote for itself rather than ones an operator authored — recognized by name ( auth token , project llm key , and bare 32 character hex reference names minted for configuration credential fields), not by a separate server flag. Those rows are shown rather than hidden so the vault's contents are fully accounted for, but nothing here offers to edit a value with no way of knowing what it is for.

title: Users and roles
text: Users and Roles are two related admin pages: Users acts on individual accounts, and Roles defines what each role is allowed to do. Manage users Open Users in the admin console. The table lists every account on the deployment, with search. Search by name or e mail. From the row menu: delete the account, grant or revoke the global admin role, or suspend/unsuspend it. A suspended account cannot sign in. Open the activity drawer for a per user view built on the same audit data as the Audit Trail page. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Invitations do not have a dedicated accept invite page. A new member accepts an invite by signing in; the invite is resolved by matching their identity on first login. Edit roles and permissions Open Roles . It shows a permission matrix across three scopes, each a tab: Central — the administration mode roles used across the deployment (the ones this admin console itself is gated on). Public Project — roles available inside the shared public project. Support Project — roles for the support project, if one is configured for this deployment. If none is configured, this tab reports that rather than an empty grid. Click a cell to grant or revoke that permission for that role, within the selected scope. Use the controls above the matrix. A new standard role only reaches projects that already exist once you use Apply to Projects next to it — creating the role does not retroactively push it everywhere by itself. The super admin column is disabled for anyone who is not a super admin, in the console only — this is a display convenience, not an enforced rule. The server does not treat super admin specially beyond the permission checks that apply to any other role.

title: GitOps with ArgoCD
text: deploy/argocd/ is the GitOps composition for the Kubernetes path: one root Application that renders every child Application under deploy/argocd/applications/ , in sync wave order. There is no umbrella Helm chart — an earlier one ( deploy/helm/elitea platform/ ) was scaffolded and never built, and was removed once app of apps replaced it. Apply the root once This is the only object you apply by hand. kubectl apply f deploy/argocd/ (no R ) reaches only this file — the children come from ArgoCD reading the directory, not from a second kubectl apply . The root itself is deliberately not one of the children it manages: an Application that enumerated itself could prune itself. Sync wave order | Application | Chart | Wave | Namespace | Why this order | | | | | | | | elitea nats | deploy/helm/nats | 2 | elitea gateway | Must be healthy before its JetStream assets are created. | | elitea nats bootstrap | deploy/helm/nats bootstrap | 1 | elitea gateway | Creates the KV buckets and budget deltas stream the gateway's counters and the scheduler both dial; the hook Job is idempotent, safe on every sync. | | elitea | deploy/helm/elitea | 0 | elitea | The platform release. | Ordering within the elitea Application is Helm hook ordering, not a further sync wave — the migration Job runs pre install,pre upgrade and Helm blocks the release on it, the workload session Job follows, and the runtime Redis consumer groups are created post install . A failed migration aborts the release and the previous pods keep serving. Where each value comes from deploy/argocd/applications/elitea.yaml states every value in one spec.source.helm block — nothing reaches the release from anywhere else: valueFiles: [values.yaml] , read from the chart's own repository path. postgresql.existingSecret and postgresql.key — the one database Secret every component derives its DATABASE URL from. llmGateway.env.GATEWAY SELF LLM ORIGINS and llmGateway.egressPosture ship empty in git on purpose — neither can get a safe chart default. Left empty, the chart refuses to render and the Application reports SyncFailed naming the field, rather than installing a gateway with a disarmed guard. Fill the two empty parameters in your own GitOps copy of the file, or imperatively: No secret goes in a parameter. A Helm parameter renders into a ConfigMap, readable by anyone with get on the namespace — the database DSN and every other sensitive value are Kubernetes Secrets that postgresql.existingSecret , runtime.material.secretName and the rest only name . Overriding values per environment To point an environment at a different capability set — values standalone.yaml or your own file — add it to spec.source.helm.valueFiles in that environment's copy of elitea.yaml , after values.yaml (Helm merges files in list order, so later files win): Keep one Application manifest per environment (a staging/elitea.yaml , a prod/elitea.yaml , or separate branches/paths per ArgoCD Application 's targetRevision ) rather than templating the Application itself — the file is already the full statement of what an environment installs. Image tag promotion Every first party image and every chart is stamped with the same release version by .github/workflows/publish.yml 's semantic release run — one tag for the whole platform, because a per component tag could only ever express a mistake. Promoting a release is changing the chart version an Application pulls: The published chart's own image.tag already defaults to the chart's version — only override image.tag to pin an environment behind the chart's own release, or to test a release candidate. Rollback ArgoCD's own history covers a sync gone wrong: For a release level rollback (a bad image), point the Application back at a previous chart version and let selfHeal: true reconcile it — the chart's own pre install,pre upgrade migration hook still runs on the way there, so a rollback that also needs a schema rollback is a database operation, not something this reconciliation does for you. If a CI release itself failed mid publish, the rollback job in publish.yml already deleted the charts and images it had pushed, so there is nothing half published to roll back to. The reference environment is a private repo The deploy/argocd/ and deploy/helm/ in this repository are the template . The team's own reference deployment rolls from a separate, private GitOps repository that layers its own value overrides and secrets on top of what is documented here — nothing in this repository points at that environment, and nothing here assumes it exists. Copy this folder's structure into your own GitOps repository rather than looking for a fourth Application that isn't in this tree. syncPolicy.automated with prune: true and selfHeal: true is set on every Application here, including the root. Removing a file from applications/ is a production deletion of that Application and everything it manages — review those diffs as such. {/ source: deploy/argocd/app of apps.yaml:1 51; deploy/argocd/applications/elitea.yaml:1 126; deploy/argocd/applications/nats.yaml:1 31; deploy/argocd/applications/nats bootstrap.yaml:1 36; deploy/README.md:142 282 (composition decision, values table); deploy/README.md:389 431 (publish.yml stamping) /}

title: Post-install configuration
text: Once the chart has installed and you have signed in as the first administrator (see Install with Helm), most day to day configuration moves into the admin console rather than back into a values file. This page is the map of what still lives where. Identity: OIDC, SAML, SCIM Configure identity providers under Configuration › Authentication in the admin console — see Authentication for the click through. What matters at the deployment level: The first global admin is a chart/environment setting, not a console one — identity.initial global admins in the auth document, or main.env.ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS . See the Helm install guide. An OIDC only install now gets the configuration plane. Before, only a Form authentication document ( ELITEA AUTH CONFIG FILE ) composed the principal validator the configuration write path needs; now env.OIDC ISSUER URL alone composes it too, as long as ELITEA AI PROJECT ID is set. A deployment with no authentication at all is still refused, in both the chart and the binary. SCIM provisions accounts and groups at /api/v2/scim/v2 , authenticated with a personal access token; the console side is only the group to role binding (see Authentication). The first global administrator A fresh database seeds only dev@elitea.ai . On a single sign on deployment, this account has no password. Set identity.initial global admins or the equivalent environment variable before you rely on the admin console. E mail: SMTP bootstrap defaults SMTP HOST , SMTP PORT , SMTP USERNAME , SMTP PASSWORD , SMTP TLS , EMAIL FROM , EMAIL REPLY TO and PUBLIC BASE URL are a default layer , not the whole configuration. Admin → E mail writes a second layer into the database, and internal/emailsettings merges the two field by field on every send — the database wins where it has a value. Ship EMAIL FROM and PUBLIC BASE URL at minimum through main.env ; SMTP PASSWORD belongs in the secrets: block (a Secret), never as a plaintext parameter. A change in the console needs no restart or re sync — the merge runs per message. .settings is what the console stored, .effective is the merged document the next message uses, .sources names database / environment / unset per field, and .configured / .reason say whether a message can be sent. ELITEA EMAIL SUPPRESS: "true" renders every message and sends none — the setting for a shadow or staging deployment. It outranks the console. Egress allowlists Two separate allowlists guard two separate outbound paths, both fail closed by default in the dangerous direction: Names the hosts a saved provider credential's api base may point at. It is the floor : the gateway also reads egress allowlist rows from gateway.governance config (edit them at Admin → LLM Proxy → Governance , no re sync needed) and enforces the union . An authored row can only add a destination — nothing an admin authors can withdraw a host the chart named. One grammar for both sources: a bare host, host:port , a .domain wildcard, or a CIDR block. The first entry anywhere turns the restriction on — with none in either source, a credential may name any public host. A private endpoint needs its address named, not only a hostname — bifrost's SSRF safe dialer refuses RFC 1918 and loopback destinations unless an entry explicitly names a private address or block, because the gateway never resolves a name before deciding (that would reopen the DNS rebinding race the allowlist exists to close). Link local addresses ( 169.254.0.0/16 , fe80::/10 — cloud metadata endpoints) are refused no matter what the allowlist says. GET /governance/status on the gateway (proxied at GET /api/v2/admin/gateway/status , and shown on Admin → LLM Proxy → Status ) reports the merged list by source and whether a private destination is actually reachable. Governs where a tenant created webhook may dial. Unset is the safe default : every RFC 1918, ULA and loopback destination is refused, both when a webhook is created and again at dial time (the destination is re resolved, not trusted from create time). Set it only to let webhooks reach a private receiver you control; link local and multicast addresses are refused unconditionally regardless of this variable. This variable is not a named key in values.yaml — set it like any other elitea main environment variable: Budgets need GATEWAY NATS URL Admin → Budgets writes spend ceiling rows, but the LLM gateway is what enforces them, through a NATS JetStream counter — GATEWAY NATS URL names that cluster (in Kubernetes, the nats block resolved in namespace by default; cross namespace deployments need the fully qualified ....elitea gateway.svc.cluster.local form). Leave it unset and the gateway starts, logs a warning, and serves /llm with no budget enforcement : every budget write still answers 200, every limit reads back exactly as authored, Settings → Usage still reports accrued spend — and no call is ever refused. GET /governance/status 's rate limits enforceable is false exactly when this is the case, and Admin → Budgets raises its own warning banner from that field once any budget row exists. The Compose standalone stack runs no NATS service and leaves this unset deliberately, for the same reason. Worker implementation: python (default) or rust worker.implementation selects which agent worker image the chart runs; the values are not interchangeable and the chart handles the difference rather than the operator. Every catalogued toolkit type and every internal chat agent tool is available, at the cost of the larger interpreter/dependency image. This is the default in both the Helm chart and standalone stack.sh . A smaller, faster process with the platform's native agent runtime (checkpointing, step limit enforcement) and no Python dependency surface — but, as of this release, 18 toolkit types are unimplemented ( ado boards , ado plans , ado repos , ado wiki , aha , bitbucket , confluence , figma , plain gitlab , jira , PowerPoint, qtest , TestIO, TestRail, XRAY Cloud, Zephyr Enterprise, Zephyr Essential, Zephyr Scale) and six internal chat agent tools are skipped with a visible notice instead of run (Image creation, Data Analysis, Elitea MCP Tools, Planner, Swarm Mode, Smart Tools Selection). Every tile still shows, greyed with a reason, rather than disappearing. runtime.json — the worker's own configuration document — is byte identical either way; only the process and its capability surface differ. Object storage and artifacts main.env.STORAGE BACKEND / STORAGE CONTAINER point at an S3 compatible bucket. It must exist before the first sync — the readiness probe tolerates a missing bucket, but the very next boot step (setting the bucket's retention lifecycle) does not, so a missing bucket looks like a green install that then crash loops. objectInit.enabled: true creates it for a self hosted S3 compatible endpoint you administer directly (RustFS, MinIO); a managed cloud object store almost always withholds CreateBucket from an application scoped credential, so create it out of band there. DeepWiki and Inventory: disk needs Both are the same pattern — a Go subapp host serving the SPI, reaching a Python engine sidecar over a Unix socket. Both are off by default , and turning either on is two settings , not one: the component block ( deepwiki: / inventory: ) and the matching main.env.ELITEA DEEPWIKI ENABLED / ELITEA INVENTORY ENABLED with its base URL, callback origin, git allowlist and client certificate paths — elitea main is the only door to either service, so a provider nobody can reach is a Deployment doing nothing. The published elitea deepwiki / elitea inventory images carry the engine source but not its dependency closure (DeepWiki alone is roughly 92 packages). The plain image serves the SPI and refuses every tool; only the engine tag can actually run a generation, and that image is materially larger — plan disk and pull time capacity accordingly. The chart refuses the combination of runner: legacy with a non engine tag rather than installing a service that starts and then refuses everything. Each provider's scratch space ( deepwiki.scratch , sized 8Gi by default) is ephemeral clone/index space, not durable storage — a wiki publishes to PostgreSQL, and a replica that dies mid generation only loses work already being redone. ELITEA DEEPWIKI GIT ALLOWLIST / the Inventory equivalent are read fail closed by both halves (the facade and the provider); two values that disagree mean an invocation that starts and then fails. See DeepWiki and Inventory for the product facing side. Observability Traces flow over OpenTelemetry to the chart's own otelCollector (on by default, otel/opentelemetry collector contrib ), which receives OTLP from elitea main, elitea scheduler and elitea main's own tracing ingest proxy. The shipped pipeline exports to debug (log only) — swap the otelCollector.config exporter for a real sink (an OTLP/HTTP endpoint, a vendor backend) before relying on traces outliving the pod. There is no bundled Langfuse or third party APM integration; every other component's OTEL EXPORTER OTLP ENDPOINT should point at the collector's Service ( http:// :4318 in namespace). Maintenance and the banner Both are console editable under Configuration , not chart settings: a dismissible banner with its own icon/style/message, and a maintenance mode that answers 503 with a splash screen to every caller without administration access (the admin console and authentication routes stay reachable, so the window is reversible from inside itself). See Features and configuration for the click through. {/ source: deploy/README.md:343 388 (SMTP layering), deploy/README.md:766 857 (egress, GATEWAY NATS URL); services/elitea main/internal/api/webhook/ssrf.go:1 90 (webhook allowlist); deploy/helm/elitea/values.yaml:1076, 1120, 1175 (deepwiki/inventory/index types env keys), 2568 2760 (deepwiki/inventory blocks), 2896 2969 (worker.implementation), 3374 3448 (otelCollector); deploy/helm/elitea/templates/main/configmap.yaml:8,64 (main.env is a free form map) /}

title: Install with Helm
text: This walks a Kubernetes install of the elitea chart end to end. Read Production deployment overview first for the topology and what the chart does not provision. Prerequisites A Kubernetes cluster with helm v3 and kubectl configured against it. Reachable, with a superuser DSN available for the database preparation Job ( CREATE DATABASE , CREATE EXTENSION vector ). A general purpose Redis reachable from the cluster; a second, mutually authenticated TLS Redis if you turn on the runtime plane. An S3 compatible bucket, created ahead of the first sync and named by main.env.STORAGE CONTAINER . A ClusterIssuer for the internal mTLS hops (LLM gateway, DeepWiki/Inventory), if you enable those components. Secrets to create beforehand Nothing secret goes in a values file — a Helm parameter renders into a ConfigMap, readable by anyone with get on the namespace. Create these Kubernetes Secrets first; the chart only ever takes their names . Wraps each project's vault key (optional on the gateway, required on main). Generate: python3 c 'import base64, os; print(base64.urlsafe b64encode(os.urandom(32)).decode())' The database DSN, one Secret + key pair that every component reading the database (elitea main, its migration Job, the scheduler, the LLM gateway, the workload session Job) derives its DATABASE URL from. Default names: Secret elitea main db , key database url . Agent execution signing keys and listener certificates (from deploy/scripts/gen runtime certs.sh ). Required if main.runtime.enabled: true . Auth Redis password, CA, browser attempt key, PAT signing key, Form users JSON. Required if using Form or mixed authentication. Required on both main and gateway; must be identical. HMAC key for signing/verifying identity headers. Two settings with no chart default The chart refuses to render while either of these is empty — there is no safe guess for either, and a guessed value would look armed while guarding nothing: | Setting | What it is | | | | | llmGateway.env.GATEWAY SELF LLM ORIGINS | Every origin that reaches this deployment's /llm surface, public and in cluster, comma separated — e.g. https://elitea.example.com/llm/v1,http://elitea main:8080/llm/v1 . | | llmGateway.egressPosture | "allowlist" (only hosts in GATEWAY EGRESS ALLOWLIST / governance rows) or "public unrestricted" (any public host, until the first governance row narrows it). Private network reachability follows only from an entry that explicitly names a private address or block — never from the posture alone. | Also required: platform.aiProjectId , the id of the platform's public/shared project — it must name a project schema ( p ) that already exists. It fills main.env.ELITEA AI PROJECT ID , llmGateway.env.ELITEA AI PROJECT ID and web.env.VITE PUBLIC PROJECT ID at once; helm template refuses a values file where the three copies disagree. Choose a values file The chart's own defaults: a default install has no production authentication , so ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED , ELITEA PROJECT INFO ENABLED , ELITEA INDEX TYPES ENABLED and ELITEA APPLICATION SKILLS ENABLED all render off, and main.runtime.enabled is off — no chat. Start here only if you are layering capabilities on by hand. The full capability set, matching docker compose.standalone full.yml — every capability flag on, the runtime plane on (agent execution, index ingest), sized for postgresql.maxConnections: 200 across up to main.autoscaling.maxReplicas: 4 . Needs both the runtime material Secret and the auth material Secret. This is the reference production shape. The cheapest install that can seed an AI provider credential through the product's own API instead of hand written SQL: production (Form) authentication plus ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED , no runtime plane — no agent execution, no chat. Needs the auth material Secret and a TLS Redis ( runtimeRedis.enabled: true ), but no runtime material Secret and no worker. A minimal single replica shape (image tag shadow v0.1 , DATABASE URL / REDIS URL inlined for a throwaway environment, autoscaling and the pod disruption budget both off). Use it for a disposable smoke/shadow environment, not as a production starting point. Install order: nats, nats bootstrap, elitea Whether you install by hand or through ArgoCD (sync waves 2 , 1 , 0 — see GitOps with ArgoCD), the order matters: the LLM gateway's budget counters and the scheduler both dial NATS, and its JetStream assets (KV buckets, the budget deltas stream) must exist first. Idempotent hook Job that creates the KV buckets and stream: helm template catches missing prerequisites before any kubectl apply: The migration job and DB bootstrap elitea migrate runs as a pre install hook; the database may start empty. The dbInit Job (hook weight 20) handles CREATE DATABASE and CREATE EXTENSION vector before migrations run. First admin bootstrap A fresh database seeds exactly one administrator, dev@elitea.ai , with no password on a single sign on deployment — name your own account instead through identity.initial global admins (a YAML list, wins when the authentication document has one) or main.env.ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS (comma separated, the usual path for a single sign on only install with no document). An entry is oidc: , saml: , or email: (matches only when the id token asserts email verified: true ). The grant is one shot: an account that already holds any administration role is left as is; one with none receives the grant on its next sign in. provider refs is the exact value the list accepts — read it after signing in once, instead of querying the database. See Install Elitea for the browser side walkthrough of this same step. Capability flags this install serves cmd/elitea main gates whole route groups on these variables. values.yaml sets every one; values standalone.yaml is the reference production set. ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED ships empty in the base chart — helpers.tpl derives "true" automatically once any authentication is configured and ELITEA AI PROJECT ID is set; a stated value always overrides the derivation. | Flag | Default install | values standalone.yaml | Needs | | | | | | | ELITEA ARTIFACTS ENABLED | on | on | object storage configured | | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED | derived | on | any authentication and ELITEA AI PROJECT ID | | ELITEA PROJECT INFO ENABLED | off | on | production authentication | | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS MUTATION ENABLED | off | off | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED and runtime.enabled | | ELITEA INDEX TYPES ENABLED | off | on | production authentication | | ELITEA APPLICATION SKILLS ENABLED | off | on | production authentication | | ELITEA RUNTIME ENABLED ( main.runtime.enabled ) | off | on | production authentication and runtime material | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS MUTATION ENABLED stays off in every shipped values file. It composes a second, asynchronous write route that would win the path from the compatibility route every install currently serves — and the compatibility route already writes status ok inline from the same admission decision, which is what makes a saved credential usable. Turning it on is a separate cutover with its own client side work, not a fix for an invisible credential. Post install checks Point your orchestrator's liveness/readiness probes here, not at an authenticated route. /admin/app — sign in as the account you named above. /docs/ (this site) and /api/docs (the OpenAPI UI) should both resolve once main.ingress (or your own edge rules) route them. See Troubleshooting for what each endpoint answers and the application level Health tab it complements. What a Kubernetes install does NOT give you No chart provisions either. The migration hook fails against a cluster where they do not already exist or where the Secret/host settings have not been pointed at them. No Ingress renders until main.ingress.enabled: true . A cluster serving the web app needs per route rules to avoid the SPA backend swallowing them. NATS and the gateway live in elitea gateway ; the rest live in elitea . LLM GATEWAY URL and GATEWAY NATS URL must be fully qualified ( ....elitea gateway.svc.cluster.local ) — short names do not resolve across namespaces. Gateway cert issues into elitea gateway ; main runs in elitea . Either colocate or replicate via reflector or external secrets. Every sensitive value is a Kubernetes Secret you provision out of band — see "Secrets to create beforehand" above. Continue to GitOps with ArgoCD to run this same install declaratively, or Configuration for the operator facing settings after the pods are Ready. {/ source: deploy/README.md:232 341 (values table, first admin), deploy/README.md:389 431 (distribution), deploy/README.md:433 605 (capability flags), deploy/README.md:607 730 (runtime + auth material), deploy/README.md:859 918 (what K8s does not give you); deploy/helm/elitea/values standalone.yaml:1 30, 105 260; deploy/helm/elitea/values auth minimal.yaml:1 70; deploy/helm/elitea/values staging.yaml:1 25; deploy/helm/elitea/values.yaml:344 360, 2306 2358 (secrets); deploy/argocd/applications/elitea.yaml:11 18 (hook ordering); deploy/helm/elitea/templates/main/migrate job.yaml, templates/worker/runtime session job.yaml, templates/dbInit/job.yaml, templates/runtimeRedis/bootstrap job.yaml (hook weights) /}

title: Day-2 operations
text: Running the platform after install: upgrading it safely, changing its master key, scaling its four independently scaled components, and where to look when something breaks. Upgrades Point your ArgoCD Application (or helm upgrade ) at the new published chart version — see GitOps with ArgoCD. The published chart's image.tag already tracks that version. elitea migrate is a pre install,pre upgrade Helm hook. Helm applies and awaits every such hook — including the migration Job — before it touches any of the release's other resources, so new pods never roll against an un migrated schema. A failed migration aborts the release , and the previously running pods keep serving; nothing is torn down until the new version proves it can start. Or, under ArgoCD, let selfHeal: true reconcile the bumped targetRevision /parameter automatically. helm rollback elitea (or the ArgoCD equivalent, argocd app rollback elitea ) returns to the previous release's values and image tags. The migration hook runs again on the way there — a rollback that also needs a schema rollback is a database operation this mechanism does not perform for you. Changing SECRETS MASTER KEY The key has three states, and moving between them is not symmetric: | State | Effect | | | | | Set, valid | Every project's vault key is wrapped with it; rows are Fernet tokens. | | Not set | The service still starts, with a log warning — every project key is stored in the clear . Anyone who can read the database can open every project secret. | | Set, malformed | The service refuses to start , naming the variable. | Rows written under one key (or under no key) do not become readable when the key changes — there is no in place re encryption. To rotate the key: run scripts/rewrap centry vault.py against a copy of the database first. It rewraps the project key and never rewrites the secret values themselves, so a rotation that fails partway leaves the plaintext secrets untouched. Both elitea main and elitea llm gateway read the same centry.secrets key table. Give the same value to every service that reads it — two services with two answers would put two row formats in one table, and neither could read what the other wrote. Scaling Three components carry a native HorizontalPodAutoscaler ; the fourth uses a different mechanism on purpose: CPU/memory HPA, minReplicas: 2 / maxReplicas: 10 by default. Scaling this past what postgresql.maxConnections was sized for is refused at render time — see Production deployment overview. CPU/memory HPA. Stateless; a rollout is safe at any time. An HPA on a custom /llm SSE connection metric — CPU/memory is a poor signal for I/O bound streaming. Off by default : it needs the Prometheus Adapter installed and configured to surface that gauge metric, or it reports FailedGetPodsMetric and silently pins at minReplicas . No native HPA. An agent execution spends most of its life waiting on a model, so CPU/memory never reflects backlog. Queue depth autoscaling through KEDA is available ( worker.autoscaling , off by default) — it scales on the Redis consumer group's pending entry depth. The chart refuses to install a KEDA ScaledObject unless KEDA is actually present, rather than creating an object nothing reads. KEDA's scaler must be able to verify the runtime Redis's private CA — install the KEDA operator with that CA mounted first. A scaler that cannot connect reports no depth, which scales the fleet down while the backlog grows; the chart cannot detect this for you. The agent worker's own replica count stays correct at 1 — the database enforces one active claim per execution regardless ( execution claims active idx is unique on (execution id, generation) while a claim is live) — but scaling out is not free capacity by default. Measure the Redis consumer group's read rate before raising it or turning KEDA on; a long cooldownSeconds (300s default) is deliberate, because an in flight agent execution can run for minutes and a short cooldown turns every quiet moment into a round of terminations. Backups Not provisioned or backed up by any chart here — bring your own PostgreSQL operator/managed service and its backup mechanism. The connection budget reserves headroom ( reservedConnections: 25 ) explicitly for backup tooling and interactive psql alongside the application's own pools, so a backup job does not compete with the application for its last connection slot. Also brought by you — the chart only creates the bucket (optionally, via objectInit ) and sets its retention lifecycle. Use your object store's own versioning/replication for backup. The nats and nats bootstrap charts are commodity infrastructure this platform points at; back up the JetStream KV buckets and stream through NATS's own tooling if their loss matters to you. Losing the JetStream store resets budget enforcement counters to zero, but does not lose spend history: the Usage page's accumulators are written independently by elitea scheduler's write back consumer from the gateway's billing deltas, not read out of the counter itself. runtime session init (or the Helm workload session Job) is what authorizes the agent worker's certificate identity in elitea runtime.workload sessions ; a database restored from a backup that predates it has no such row. Re run standalone stack.sh seed runtime (compose) or re trigger the workload session hook Job (Helm) to recover, rather than assuming a restore alone brings chat back. CI/CD: what publishes, and how it's checked .github/workflows/publish.yml runs on pushes to main / next : semantic release decides the version, then every first party image is built, scanned twice (once against the artefact this release actually pushes, in addition to a same day CI scan of a rebuild), and cosign signed keylessly before the charts ( elitea , nats , nats bootstrap ) are packaged, stamped with that version, pushed to oci://ghcr.io/elitea ng/charts/ , and signed the same way. The chart job runs strictly after the images it references are pushed, so a chart never reaches the registry pointing at a tag that does not exist yet. If any stage fails, a rollback job deletes everything that stage's run had already pushed — charts and images alike. Separately, .github/workflows/helm install smoke.yml installs the chart into a real kind cluster (not just helm template ) on every PR touching deploy/helm/ , and asserts every pod reaches Ready, the DeepWiki/Inventory provider pod's two containers run the runners the chart set, the facade's provider registration is healthy over its mTLS hop, and a fixture generation completes end to end — the runtime plane, workers and LLM gateway stay off in that smoke run, so it proves the chart installs cleanly, not the full product. Security posture Every published image is scanned by Trivy against the exact digest this release pushes (not a same day rebuild), gated by scripts/ci/image scan gate.sh ; an exempted finding must be recorded in .github/image scan exempt.txt rather than silently passing. The agent execution plane's three listeners (control, output, content) all require and verify a client certificate; there is no cleartext mode. The runtime and auth material both arrive as Kubernetes Secrets, copied by an init container into an owner only emptyDir because a plain Secret volume cannot satisfy the permission profile the code enforces. The edge (Ingress/HTTPRoute) must strip caller supplied X Auth and X Elitea identity headers before they reach elitea main — the pod network typically sits inside trusted proxy cidrs , so anything reaching the Service with these headers set by the caller is an impersonation. main.ingress.stripIdentityHeaders lists the exact set for the HTTPRoute path; a plain networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress has no portable header removal field and must strip them on the ingress controller itself. Required, not optional, on both elitea main and the gateway, and the two must agree — see Install with Helm. Troubleshooting Operator facing infrastructure checks ( /healthz , /readyz , the application level Health tab, common agent/pipeline/toolkit errors) live on one page: see Troubleshooting. This page covers the deployment mechanics around those checks; that one covers what each check actually reports. {/ source: deploy/README.md:920 976 (SECRETS MASTER KEY three states, rewrap script), deploy/README.md:163 231 (hook ordering, migration abort behaviour); deploy/helm/elitea/values.yaml:80 136 (connection budget/reservedConnections), 1567 1573, 1702 1712, 2452 2532 (main/web/gateway HPAs), 2896 3070 (worker.implementation, KEDA autoscaling); .github/workflows/publish.yml:1 20, 155 177, 361 431, 718 934 (release pipeline, scan then sign, chart packaging); .github/workflows/helm install smoke.yml:1 70 (what the smoke job proves); deploy/README.md:632 679 (runtime material init container), deploy/README.md:106 111 (runtime session init recovery) /}

title: Production deployment overview
text: Elitea's Kubernetes path is one Helm chart, elitea , composed with two supporting charts ( nats , nats bootstrap ) through ArgoCD's app of apps pattern — there is no umbrella chart. This page is the map; Install with Helm walks the install itself. A one host Compose stack ( docker compose.standalone full.yml ) runs the same topology for evaluation and small teams — see Install Elitea. This section covers the Kubernetes path only. Target topology Every arrow into the worker and the runtime Redis is mutually authenticated (mTLS or a TLS Redis ACL) — that plane's material is described in Install with Helm and deploy/runtime/README.md . DeepWiki and Inventory are two instances of the same subapp host pattern: a Go host process reaching a Python engine sidecar over a Unix socket inside one pod. What the chart creates, and what you bring The chart is one release — elitea main and its migration Job, elitea web, the scheduler, the LLM gateway, the agent worker, the runtime Redis, the OTel collector, the database preparation Job, and (opt in) the DeepWiki and Inventory provider services with their own migration Jobs. nats and nats bootstrap are separate charts, synced first. No chart provisions it. Point postgresql.existingSecret at a Secret holding the DSN; the database may start empty (the migration Job bootstraps the schema itself), but a superuser DSN is still needed for CREATE DATABASE and CREATE EXTENSION vector . Two separate instances: a plaintext general purpose Redis (sessions, project SSE) and, only if the runtime plane is on, a mutually authenticated TLS Redis for agent dispatch. Neither is provisioned by this chart. The nats and nats bootstrap charts ship the coordination substrate the LLM gateway's budget counters and the scheduler dial — install them, but they are commodity infrastructure this chart points at rather than owns. An S3 compatible endpoint for artifacts and DeepWiki/Inventory output. The bucket must exist before the first sync (or set objectInit.enabled: true for a self hosted S3 compatible store you administer directly); a missing bucket lets the deployment look green and then crash loop on the next boot step. No Ingress or HTTPRoute renders until main.ingress.enabled is on, and even then it is one / rule with elitea main as the sole backend — see Install with Helm for the edge caveat. The chart consumes an authentication configuration document or OIDC ISSUER URL ; it issues no certificates of its own beyond the in cluster mTLS hops (cert manager ClusterIssuer , brought by you). Sizing: the PostgreSQL connection budget The runtime plane (agent execution) opens six isolated connection pools per elitea main replica — 36 connections beyond the primary pool — and they may not share capacity. values standalone.yaml sizes for this explicitly: at postgresql.maxConnections: 200 and main.autoscaling.maxReplicas: 4 , four replicas cost roughly 4 × 42 = 168 connections, inside the 175 left after reservedConnections: 25 (interactive psql , backup tooling, the migration and dbInit Jobs). The chart's own guard ( elitea main.validateConnectionBudget ) refuses to render a topology that would exceed the stated ceiling, rather than letting it surface later as FATAL: sorry, too many clients already on whichever component connects next. A connection pooler is not a substitute for this budget today. pgbouncer in transaction mode breaks pgx's prepared statement caching and the secrets backfill's advisory lock; session mode buys almost nothing because this platform's client pools already hold connections open for their lifetime. Size PostgreSQL for the topology instead. Published artefacts Every chart ( elitea , nats , nats bootstrap ) and every first party image is built, cosign signed (keyless) and pushed to ghcr.io/elitea ng by the release job in .github/workflows/publish.yml , after the images they reference are already pushed and signed. An OCI chart reference resolves by SemVer, so version is required in practice — there is no floating tag to fall back on. The in repo chart defaults to "latest" ; the published chart's image.tag is rewritten to the release version so it never installs a stale cached layer. Image manifests verify the same way, against ghcr.io/elitea ng/ : . If any part of a release fails, the rollback job deletes the pushed charts along with the images — a chart never stays published pointing at an image that got rolled back. Continue to Install with Helm for the step by step install, or GitOps with ArgoCD if you are deploying through the app of apps. {/ source: deploy/README.md:163 431 (chart table, composition decision, distribution); deploy/helm/elitea/values standalone.yaml:1 20 (connection budget); deploy/helm/elitea/values.yaml:80 136 (postgresql.maxConnections, reservedConnections); deploy/helm/elitea/Chart.yaml (chart description) /}

title: Backend services and workers
text: This page covers the day to day loop for elitea main , elitea llm gateway , elitea scheduler and the two agent workers: running against a real database, writing a migration, editing the OpenAPI spec, and testing a worker in isolation. Run elitea main against the compose database Bring up just the infrastructure services from the standalone stack ( certs , then up ), then run elitea main from source against them: task run does the same thing without a custom DATABASE URL , against whatever the process environment already points at. Integration tests against a real database Tests gated on ELITEA TEST DATABASE URL skip themselves (with a message naming the variable) when it is unset, so task test stays green without a database and exercises the real thing once you supply one: Point it at the standalone stack's PostgreSQL, or any disposable PostgreSQL with the vector extension available — most of these tests provision and drop their own per run database or schema, so they do not need an empty server. Migrations Migration files live under services/elitea main/migrations/ , in three independently ordered scopes: shared/ , tenant/ and agentstate/ (embedded and loaded by the internal/infra/db/migrate package). A separate, single file directory — internal/infra/db/migrations/001 initial.sql — carries only the legacy pylon era initial schema, applied first when a database doesn't already have it. Each versioned file is named NNNN description.sql and identified by a SHA 256 checksum of its contents — a migration is checksum immutable once it exists : never edit an applied file, always add a new one with the next free number. Reads the base branch as origin holds it now and fails if your new migration's number is not above its highest. This catches two authors picking the same free number independently — a collision that is only visible once both branches merge. shared/ for cross tenant tables, tenant/ for anything created once per project schema ( p ), agentstate/ for the separate agent state database. Mixing scopes in one file is not supported — LoadManifest rejects a nested directory or a filename that doesn't match NNNN name.sql . TestEmbeddedHistoriesHaveExpectedHeads in internal/infra/db/migrate/manifest test.go pins the expected head version per scope. A new highest numbered migration in a scope that test already covers needs the pin updated in the same change. Editing the OpenAPI spec services/elitea main/api/openapi/v2.yaml is the single source both the Go server and the TypeScript client generate from. A change to it ripples through several checked gates, in this order: Runs oapi codegen into services/elitea main/internal/api/generated/api.gen.go . ci go.yml 's "Verify generated OpenAPI server is current" step re runs the same command and fails the build on any git diff . Writes src/shared/api/generated/ . scripts/check generated client.mjs fails a stale client — see elitea web development. Add or amend the corresponding entry in apps/elitea web/src/shared/api/endpoints.manifest.json by hand — it is asserted against the generated client, not generated from the spec itself. TestCurrentMainRoutePublicRulesMatchPinnedCatalog ( services/elitea main/internal/api/main public rules test.go ) pins every route pattern's authentication rule against a fixed catalog. A renamed or added public path needs an entry there too. The LLM gateway services/elitea llm gateway is a separate Go module (Go 1.26), deliberately outside the root go.work . Build and test it from inside its own directory, with the workspace explicitly disabled: ci gateway.yml runs its own pipeline for this module; task test / task vet / task lint at the repository root never open it, and a green root level run is not evidence about it. Worker test recipes Runs python m pytest services/elitea worker python/tests against whatever elitea sdk build is installed in your environment. Plain pip , no uv lockfile. ci python.yml runs a stricter recipe for SDK conformance coverage: it clones elitea sdk at a pinned revision, verifies that revision's archive checksum, cherry picks four named patches onto it, and installs the result with one pip install pass — reproduce that only if you are changing SDK compatibility behavior, not for an ordinary worker change.
